name: Yimas
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Yimas stress is essentially predictable by a simple rule: assign primary stress to the first syllable of the word, and secondary stress to the third syllable, if the word is longer than three syllables. Stress is not phonemic. (Foley 1991:75)

tone_statements.citation: [author not shown in the record seen] 2011. Tonal Diversity in Languages of Papua New Guinea. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-008. Dallas: SIL International. (PDF on sil.org)
tone_statements.quote: The variation in suprasegmentals is correspondingly diverse. Some languages have predictable stress—for example, Yimas (Foley 1991:75ff.), Hua (Haiman 1980), Awtuw (Feldman 1986:15ff.), Bukiyip (Conrad 1991), Au (Scorza 1978:9), Tauya (MacDonald 1990:84), Ono (Phinnemore 1976), and Urii (Webb 1974), among others. Some languages are reported to have contrastive stress, such as Korafe (Farr and Farr 1974), Faiwol (Mecklenburg 1974), and Samo (Daniel and Shaw 1977). [...] Some have what may be labeled a pitch-accent system, e.g., Tinputz (Hostetler and Hostetler 1975) [...] many languages are definitely tonal.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification now. If Foley 1991:75-80 (or Peng 2013's reproduction of his data) shows alternating secondaries in 6+-syllable words, n=6-8 would change 101000/1010000/10100000 -> 101010/1010100/10101010 and 'kind' fixed-strict -> binary iterative (trochaic L-to-R, non-degenerate); n=2-5 cells (10, 100, 1010, 10100) are secure either way.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: the deciding text is the StressTyp2 entry(Foley 1991:75), confirmed verbatim in the held together with passage 2079 and 12 stress-marked word forms; Foley 1991 itself is not yet obtained, so the check stops at the database transcription. (2) Source: the classification ultimately rests on the right work (Foley 1991, the sole reference grammar; no phonology article, dissertation or instrumental study of Yimas prosody exists per Glottolog's single descriptive ref, the 2026-08-18 lit review search, and archive.org/OpenLibrary/ROA checks now), but only second-hand: a survey excerpt, a course blog, and now Alderete 1999. (3) What the held and downloaded material shows: every channel agrees on n=2-5 (initial primary; trisyllables 100 per Foley's 'if the word is longer than three syllables', StressTyp2 forms ˈawtmayŋi/ˈyamparan, Alderete fn. 8; 4-syll 1010 wúratàkay; 5-syll 10100 mámantàkarman

sources.citation: Alderete, John. 1999. Head dependence in stress-epenthesis interaction. In B. Hermans & M. van Oostendorp (eds.), The Derivational Residue in Phonological Optimality Theory, 29-50. Amsterdam: John Benjamins. [Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-453 preprint, 10 pp.]
sources.quote: 'In Yimas, the main stress regularly falls on the initial syllable of a word (3a). Epenthesis into this position ... push[es] stress forward a syllable (3b)' with data wáŋkaŋ, kúlanaŋ, wúratàkay (1010), mámantàkarman (5 syll = 10100), pɨkám, tɨmí, and 'if the vowels of both the first and second syllable are derived by epenthesis, then main stress defaults to the initial syllable' (krɨ́mkɨnawt, tɨ́mpɨnàwkwan). fn. 6: 'Secondary stress is assigned to the third syllable from the beginning of the word, suggesting that stress obeys a binary pattern.' p. 13: 'Secondary stress is assigned to every ot
